old_title: Ukraine war live: Nato will destroy 'everything' used by Putin if he attacks
new_title: Ukraine war live: Nato member blames Putin after two ships struck in Black Sea

Nato's top commander bluntly warned Russia on Monday that his forces would destroy "anything and everything" involved in any attack if Moscow is "foolish enough" to launch an assault.
US air force general Alexus Grynkewich, outlining his 'theory of victory' at a security conference in Warsaw, said the defensive alliance would block, blunt and break any attack on any member.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be."
"We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile."
European governments have accused Moscow of using sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them and Russia warned last month it would use nuclear weapons if Nato attempted to cut off its exclave of Kaliningrad.
Meanwhile Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky demanded his US counterpart Donald Trump pressure Russia to honour an energy ceasefire after alleging Moscow attacked Ukrainian infrastructure overnight.
Zelensky said such strikes continued hours after Trump announced that Russia had agreed to a limited ceasefire on energy targets. The Kremlin has yet to confirm or deny those claims.
Ukraine hits back over Russia's claims it 'doesn't deserve a ceasefire'
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, writing on social media, pushes back on his Russian counterpart's assertion that Volodymyr Zelensky "has not earned a respite on the battlefield".
"Lavrov, however, has already earned a front-row seat at the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression," Sybiha writes. "The more irrelevant and cynical comments - the more evidence for the Tribunal."
Sergei Lavrov had suggested the Ukrainian president was undeserving of an energy ceasefire as announced by US president Donald Trump.
Trump defends diesel deal with Russia amid backlash
Donald Trump appeared to defend Friday's announcement of a controversial diesel deal with Russia.
Writing on Truth Social on Monday, he said: "The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story. I made the right choice for the American People - ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST! President DONALD J. TRUMP"
The Helsinki-based think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates that the EU has paid €238bn ($266bn) to import Russian fossil fuels since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
The latest: Zelensky demands Trump pressure on Putin after 'energy ceasefire breached'
Volodymyr Zelensky has demanded that US president Donald Trump pressure Russia to honour the ceasefire after alleging that Moscow's overnight attack targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
"Americans must make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire," he said. "We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief so we can achieve an energy ceasefire," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said such strikes continued hours after Trump announced that Russia had agreed to a limited ceasefire on energy targets. The Kremlin has yet to confirm or deny those claims.
Power outages were reported overnight in parts of Ukraine following ongoing Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, including a power plant. Zelensky on Monday said Kyiv was willing to honour the energy ceasefire if Russia agrees to it as well. "We agree if they agree," he said. "We have already shown that we mean it. Last night Russian oil refineries were not attacked," he added.
Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system, Purl, that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to stop its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Germany's Merz says Russia not serious about peace, calls for tougher sanctions
Russia has shown that it is not serious about peace talks by responding to the US proposal for an energy ceasefire with fresh attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, said German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Monday.
"Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia," said Merz. "Following Moscow's ruthless attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, we must actually tighten them further."
People are rejoicing about the removal of Russian bots from social media - but the truth is far more complicated
Social media is busy with claims that something dramatic just happened to the online environment.
Huge numbers of posts claim that Russian bot traffic has fallen dramatically across the internet. And, with that, so has the number of posts and replies from automated accounts on sites such as X, formerly Twitter, and Facebook, the posts claim.
It has led to something of a trend on X, in which users post what they call a "bot test": an opinion or claim of the kind that would ordinarily lead to an influx of automated responses. Some users do indeed claim that they have seen a substantial reduction in the number of replies of a certain kind, and use that to suggest both that the previous responses were from automated accounts and that those accounts have reduced in number.
More here.
Europe should impose more sanctions on Russia, says Poland's Tusk
European countries should increase sanctions on Russia and all Western nations should show their solidarity with Ukraine, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.
"Russia is not interested in a ceasefire, de-escalation, or peace... that is why I will go to Brussels to urge all European partners to consider increasing sanctions," Tusk told the Warsaw Security Forum.
"Ukraine cannot be broken or intimidated. Poland cannot be intimidated. The world cannot be broken or intimidated. That signal must go out today from every capital, from Warsaw to Washington."
EU foreign policy chief doubts Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
The European Union's top diplomat on Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg. "Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy."
Kallas also pushed back on Trump's comments on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and that Zelensky has not done enough to end the war. She said that now is not the time to hold elections in Ukraine, at least not without a ceasefire.
On Monday, Zelensky said holding elections in Ukraine was impossible during war time, especially with new Russian tactics involving attacks during both the day and night.
He added, however, that he would be ready to work towards doing so if Ukraine secured a full ceasefire lasting at least 60 days.
Kremlin offers one-day ceasefire for Ukraine to hold election
Russian president Vladimir Putin would be ready to order his forces not to attack Ukraine during a presidential election - but only on the day of the vote itself, according to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
The Kremlin earlier rejected a 60-day ceasefire idea proposed by Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky to allow his country to hold presidential elections, claiming it wants an overall peace deal instead.
Zelensky backs 'energy ceasefire', but no confirmation from Putin
Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will support a bilateral "energy ceasefire" with Russia, after being caught off guard by Donald Trump's shock announcement that a deal had already been agreed.
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, the US president said: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
The Ukrainian president said he had not heard of such a deal, but would agree to it if Russia did, according to Axios. Kyiv had publicly backed a truce on striking energy infrastructure before Trump announced on Friday plans to lift sanctions on Moscow to supply diesel to the US and global markets - much to Zelensky's chagrin.
The Kremlin has yet to acknowledge Trump's claim to have established a ceasefire between the warring sides. Russia had reportedly sought sanctions relief as a concession for its adherence to a ceasefire earlier in the week.
The controversial diesel deal with Russia has proven controversial even within Trump's own base as the president looks to bring down energy prices in the US ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump hit out at Zelensky on Saturday, saying it was time for Ukraine to find a new leader after Kyiv struck Russian oil refineries. Zelensky said on Sunday he would hold new elections if Putin agrees to a 60-day "total ceasefire".
Zelensky says EU to provide €3bn in military funding this week
The EU will disburse almost €3bn (£2.5bn) in defence support to Ukraine this week as part of its €90bn (£76bn) support loan, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said.
"We deeply appreciate every concrete step taken to support our defense and our people," Zelensky said.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, EU countries have provided €200bn (£169 bn) in economic, financial, and military support to Ukraine and approved €90bn (£76bn) more over the next two years as an EU support loan.

Drones struck two merchant vessels in the Black Sea off Bulgaria this morning, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations.
Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev said Russia was likely responsible for the strikes, and that five crew members from one ship were injured. The fate of the crew of the second vessel was unclear, though Radev said one member had been found alive after it sank.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attacks near the coast of Nato member Bulgaria and called for "those responsible" to be held accountable.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable," von der Leyen said on X.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump insisted yesterday that an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia was still holding, even as Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of relentless attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities.
When pressed about the ongoing attacks by Russia, Trump refused to criticise Vladimir Putin and said there had been "violations on both sides".
Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector for the past two days, but blamed Russia for not heeding Trump's truce.
Zelensky accuses Russia of violating energy ceasefire as strikes kill four in Kharkiv
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Russia of ignoring Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire, saying Moscow has continued attacking Ukrainian energy facilities and civilian infrastructure while Kyiv has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries.
Zelensky said Russian forces had launched more than 100 weapons, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles, against Ukraine since Monday evening.
At least four people were killed and 41 injured in Kharkiv after a Russian strike destroyed a residential building, leaving rescue workers searching through the rubble overnight.
Kyiv was also targeted by five ballistic missiles that struck civilian infrastructure, Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine had received no advance warning from its partners.
"Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues," he said.
The Ukrainian leader said Kyiv had not attacked Russian oil refineries or other energy infrastructure in the two days since Trump announced the ceasefire, but Moscow had continued its strikes across 19 Ukrainian regions.
Zelensky reiterated that Ukraine remained prepared to take reciprocal steps towards de-escalation but called for greater international pressure on Moscow.
"Wars end when the aggressor realises that it cannot prolong the war," he said, warning that direct or indirect support for Russia and delays in military assistance to Ukraine would undermine efforts to achieve peace.
Zelensky says Ukraine bombed Russian data centers to take out social media bots dividing the west
Three killed, 16 wounded in Ukrainian attacks on Russia's Belgorod, governor says
Three people have been killed and 16 wounded in Ukrainian attacks on Russia's Belgorod region which borders Ukraine, the local governor said on Wednesday.
Two people were killed in an overnight attack and another man died following an attack that took place on Friday, the region's governor, Alexander Shuvaev, said.
Finland criticises Trump's Russian diesel deal
Finland's foreign minister Elina Valtonen has criticised Donald Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, warning that providing Moscow with additional revenue would help fuel its war in Ukraine.
Speaking to Reuters at a forum in Singapore on Tuesday, Valtonen said feeding Russia's "imperial" war machine with more money was "not a good idea".
She urged the US, as the leader of the free world, to stand with Ukraine in its fight against Russian aggression.
"The rest of the world should be on the side of the victim and certainly those countries who want to still be strong for the concept of freedom," she said.
Valtonen also called on European Union member states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens until Moscow ends its war in Ukraine.
"I hear from all of my colleagues in the European Union an agreement to the principle and I am so sure that all of the European Union countries will start restricting tourist visas to Russians even more strongly now, especially because Russia is also waging a hybrid war against Europe," she said.
Poland accuses Russia of arson attack on Starlink station as two arrested
Poland has accused Russian intelligence services of orchestrating an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station near Warsaw, as authorities arrested two Turkish nationals suspected of carrying out the sabotage.
The suspects were detained in Germany in connection with the 23 September attack on Starlink infrastructure in Wola Krobowska, about 40km south of the Polish capital, officials said on Monday.
"We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage," Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's minister overseeing intelligence services, said in a news release, adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly turning to people with ties to the criminal underworld.
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk described the incident as "another act of hybrid warfare".
Speaking at a security conference in Warsaw on Tuesday, Mr Siemoniak warned that Russian intelligence services were carrying out almost "daily acts of subversion" against European countries supporting Ukraine.
"There is not a week where activities do not happen," he said, adding that Moscow had increasingly relied on recruits contacted through platforms such as Telegram to carry out attacks.
"Our enemy - that is Russia's intelligence services - changes its methods of operation and has unlimited resources," he said.
The Starlink incident is among more than 210 suspected acts of sabotage and other hostile activities across Europe tracked by the Associated Press since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Western officials believe such operations are intended to undermine support for Kyiv, spread fear and instability across Europe and stretch security resources.
Norway's domestic intelligence chief, Beate Gangas, also warned of the growing threat, telling the conference: "We are in the most serious situation since the Second World War."
Zelensky says Ukraine halted strikes on Russian oil refineries
Ukraine halted strikes on Russian oil refineries and its other energy infrastructure for two days following US president Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday.
But he said that Russia failed to refrain from strikes.
"During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine," he said on X.
He said the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different weapons - jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine still receiving intelligence data from US, foreign minister says
Ukraine continues to receive intelligence data from the United States, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday, seeking to calm concerns after his country received no warnings before Russia fired ballistic missiles at Kyiv.
Speaking during the Warsaw Security Forum, Sybiha said Kyiv and Washington were continuing their cooperation.
He reiterated an appeal for more air defence systems and also energy equipment supplies as Ukraine braces for another winter with Russia waging war on the country.
Eleven sailors missing after drones strike ships off Bulgaria
Eleven sailors are missing after the drone strikes on two merchant vessels off Bulgaria this morning, according to officials.
Officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets. Bulgarian media identified the vessel as the cargo ship Azov Concord.
Another ship, the Chelsea 3 sailing under Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship - seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis - were rescued and none seriously injured.
What to know about the Nord Stream pipeline explosions trial opening in Germany this week
A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany this week over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago in one of the biggest acts of sabotage in Europe since the Second World War.
The suspect faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure, according to prosecutors.
The attack laid bare Europe's dependence on Russian energy but also raised sensitive questions about Ukraine and its Western allies.
Bulgaria summons Russian ambassador after two ships struck in Black Sea
Two ships were hit in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, sinking one and prompting emergency rescues, prime minister Rumen Radev said this morning.
Rescuers pulled all 15 crew from the Ukrainian-owned "Chelsea 3", sailing under Maltese flag, with five treated for minor injuries, Radev confirmed via social media.
The crew, comprising seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, said three aerial drones struck the vessel's deck and hull.
Radev blamed Russia for the strikes and said he would summon the Russian ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a conversation today.
